title: Changing a table things depend on
desc: Adding, retyping and dropping columns when automations and apps already read them.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can change a live table's shape — add, rename, retype or drop a column — without breaking somebody else's automation.

steps.title: Read "Used by" before you touch a column
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep's `leveranciersfacturen` table has collected supplier invoices for months. A nightly mailbox reader adds a row per invoice; a Monday reminder chases every row where `status` is still *nieuw* (new). Drop the wrong column this afternoon and the failure arrives at three in the morning, inside an automation you do not own.

So read **Used by** before you open **Columns**. The tabs are **Columns**, **Rows**, **Retention**, **Sharing** and **Used by**, and that last one carries a count: every automation, app, web page and knowledge base that touches this table, under **Where**, **Does** and **Last time**. **Does** says *reads*, *writes* or *reads and writes*. A row marked *someone else's* belongs to a colleague and is not a link you can follow.

The Columns tab repeats it per column, as a small pill on the row: *1 automation*, *3 automations*.

steps.title: Whose table is this, and may you change its shape?
steps.bodyMd:
Two things decide whether the Columns tab is yours to edit.

**Scope.** A card says **Personal** / *only this account* or **Whole organisation** / *organisation*. A personal table is deny-by-default — nobody else can read it, org administrators included, and it can never be shared — so its columns are always yours.

**Permission, for an organisation table only.** Changing an organisation table's columns needs the datatables-management permission, which the **Organisation Admin** and **Agent Admin** roles carry. An **Agent Editor** or **Member** can read and write rows all day and still not reshape the table. That check is skipped entirely for a personal table.

On top of that you must own the table: its creator, or an organisation administrator of that same organisation. Your grade is on the card — **"You own this table"**, **"You can read and change rows"**, **"You can read rows"**.

So this lesson's moves land for everyone on a table of their own, and on an organisation table only for the two roles above. If the Columns tab offers you nothing to save, that is the answer — not a bug.

steps.question: Sanne is an **Agent Editor** at Van Dijk Groep. She writes rows every week in the organisation's `leveranciersfacturen` table, and she also keeps a personal table of her own. Which columns can she change?

choices.label: Only her personal table's — reshaping an organisation table needs a permission her role does not carry.
Both — writing rows in a table is what proves she may edit it.
choices.feedback: Rows and shape are separate rungs. Her grade lets her read and change rows; columns, sharing, retention and deletion sit one rung higher, at owner, and an organisation table adds the management permission on top.

choices.label: Neither — column edits are for Organisation Admins, and a personal table is no exception.
choices.feedback: The permission check is skipped for a personal table: only her account can see it at all, so there is nobody to protect it from. She reshapes it freely.

choices.label: Both, as soon as a colleague grants her editor on the organisation table.
choices.feedback: A grant only ever carries viewer or editor — it cannot hand over ownership, and it cannot hand over an organisation permission either. Someone with the Organisation Admin or Agent Admin role has to make that change.

steps.explanation: Two gates, in order: you must own the table, and — for an organisation table only — hold the datatables-management permission that the Organisation Admin and Agent Admin roles carry. A personal table skips the second gate, which is why everyone can practise these moves on a table of their own.

steps.title: Adding is safe. Dropping and retyping are not.
steps.bodyMd:
Five edits. Only two of them cost you anything.

- **Add** a column and nothing notices: existing rows get an empty cell, and no automation reads a column it has never heard of.
- **Rename** one and only the label changes. A column that has already been saved keeps the technical key your automations name, so they keep working.
- **Reorder** with the drag handle: free.
- **Remove** a column and its values disappear from every row.
- **Retype** one and every value is rewritten — anything that does not fit the new type is lost.

Only those last two open the dialog **This throws away data**, with the buttons **Save anyway** and **Keep them**.

steps.question: You remove `status` from Van Dijk Groep's invoice table and press Save columns. Bee Flow stops you before anything is written. What has it looked at?

choices.label: Which automations still name that column — and the save goes through only once you confirm it.
Whether any row still holds a value in `status`.
choices.feedback: Rows are the other line in the dialog — how many values go — not what makes the drop dangerous. A column that is empty in all 412 rows is still stopped while an automation names it.

choices.label: Whether the automation's next run succeeds, rolling the change back if it does not.
choices.feedback: Nothing waits for the next run, and nothing is rolled back later — that is precisely the failure this guard exists to prevent. It would surface at three in the morning, inside somebody else's automation.

choices.label: Whether you are the owner of the table.
choices.feedback: Ownership was settled before the editor opened; only an owner sees Save columns at all. This refusal is about dependants, not about you.

steps.explanation: Bee Flow already knows who reads this table, so the question can be answered before anything is written: the dialog names the automations that will stop working, and the server refuses the drop again unless your confirmation comes with it. Confirm with **Save anyway** and the column goes — and the automation that named it now has to be fixed where it lives.

steps.title: "Someone else changed these columns"
steps.bodyMd:
The Columns tab loads a version number along with the columns and sends it back when you save. If the stored version has moved on, your save is refused with: **Someone else changed these columns while you were editing. Their version is now shown — please make your change again.**

Your unsaved edits are gone, their columns are on screen, and you redo your change on top of theirs. Nothing lands half-applied: the model and the actual table change together or not at all.

One catch worth knowing. An organisation's column definitions live in a single versioned document, so a colleague saving a **different** table in the same organisation can be what bumps it — at Van Dijk that is one purchasing assistant away. Keep the tab open for a moment, not for an afternoon.

steps.title: The order that never wakes anyone
steps.instruction: Van Dijk Groep wants a `betaald_op` (paid on) date column on the invoice table. Put the four moves in the safe order.

items.label: Open "Used by" and note every automation on the table, and which of them are someone else's
Add the column on the Columns tab and pick its Kind
Press "Save columns" and wait for the note "Columns saved."
Open the automation that should fill the column and point its Datatable step at it

sim.feedback: Reading "Used by" first is what makes the rest safe: you know who to warn and what to check afterwards. And the column does not exist until the save lands, so the automation cannot be pointed at it any earlier.

steps.title: What is fixed once the table exists
steps.bodyMd:
Four things sit outside the edit you are about to make.

**Reserved names.** Every table already carries `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `created_by` and `org_id`. They are not on the Columns tab, and a new column may not take one of those names.

**The technical name.** A table's **Technical name** can never be changed after creation — renaming means a new table and moving the rows across. A column's display name is the opposite: change it whenever you like, its key stays put underneath.

**Row visibility.** Whether everyone sees every row, or only whoever added it, can be narrowed but never widened back — opening it up would disclose every older row at once.

**The ceilings**, which are generous: 100 columns per table, 100 options on a "One of a list" column, 120 characters for a name.

steps.title: Your turn: plan a risky change
steps.instruction: Van Dijk Groep wants two changes to `leveranciersfacturen`: drop `opmerking` (a long-text note nobody fills in) and change `btw_pct` (the VAT rate) from Text to Number so an automation can compare it. "Used by" lists two automations — the nightly mailbox reader (*reads and writes*, marked *someone else's*) and the Monday reminder (*reads*, yours). Write the plan: what you check before saving, which change is the more dangerous one and why, what the dialog will tell you, and what happens to the colleague's automation.
steps.placeholder: e.g. First I open Used by and write down which automation reads which column, then…

steps.title: Some tables do not let you edit columns at all
steps.bodyMd:
Not every table's shape is yours to change. Van Dijk's `uren` table is mirrored from Nextcloud Tables, and its Columns tab says so: **These columns come from Nextcloud and cannot be added to, removed, renamed or retyped here. Change them in Nextcloud — the next refresh brings them here.**

A form's answers table is the same idea pointed at a form: the columns *are* the questions, so you change the form and the table follows. A "Web service answers" table has locked columns that are filled in automatically — but there you may add columns of your own alongside them.

A small lock on the row tells you which columns are not yours.

steps.question: The invoice table was created so that rows are visible only to whoever added them. Now the whole Inkoop group should see every row. What happens when you switch it over?

choices.label: It is refused: row visibility can be narrowed to the author but never opened up again — you are told to make a new table.
It applies from now on: new rows are visible to everyone, older rows stay with their author.
choices.feedback: There is no per-row memory of the old setting, so a half-way state is not on offer. That is why the switch is refused outright instead of applied.

choices.label: It goes through once you confirm it, the way a column drop does.
choices.feedback: A column drop is confirmable because you can see exactly what it costs. This one has no confirmation: nothing reopens rows that were written under the narrower promise.

choices.label: It works, but only for an organisation administrator.
choices.feedback: No role gets past it. The refusal is about disclosing rows retroactively, not about who is asking.

steps.explanation: Every existing row was added while its author was the only reader, and widening would disclose all of them at once. Like the technical name, this is a one-way door — so the answer points you at a fresh table instead, the same instinct as the column guard applied to rows.

steps.title: What does the product do?
steps.instruction: Match each move on one of Van Dijk Groep's tables to the answer you get.

pairs.left: You remove a column that two automations read
pairs.note: The dialog names the rows it costs and the automations that stop working; Save anyway lets it through.

pairs.left: You open the Columns tab of a table mirrored from a spreadsheet
pairs.note: The sheet's header row owns the shape; the next refresh brings your change across.

pairs.left: A colleague saved columns while your edit was open
pairs.right: Your save is rejected, their version shown
pairs.note: Redo your change on top of theirs — nothing lands half-applied.

pairs.left: You add a column to a table that already holds 412 rows
pairs.right: Saves straight away, new cells empty
pairs.note: Adding is additive: no dialog, and nothing that reads the table notices.

pairs.left: You rename a column that the Monday automation reads
pairs.note: A saved column keeps its technical key, which is what the automation actually names.

steps.title: Add a column — we'll verify it
steps.instruction: Open a table you own that the "Used by" tab already lists, and read that tab first. A personal table counts — an automation can read one. Then add one column on the Columns tab, give it a Kind, and press "Save columns" — you should see the note "Columns saved." and no warning dialog, because adding costs nothing. Go back to "Used by": the automation should still be sitting there.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Read "Used by" first.** It names every automation, app, web page and knowledge base on the table, whether each one *reads*, *writes* or *reads and writes*, and which are someone else's. The Columns tab marks the columns that are spoken for.
- **Know which edits are cheap.** Adding, renaming and reordering cost nothing. Removing and retyping open **This throws away data**, and a drop that breaks an automation is refused until you confirm it.
- **Expect to be interrupted.** A colleague's save can beat yours, a mirrored table refuses column edits altogether, and row visibility narrows but never widens. Each refusal tells you what to do instead.
- **Know whether the tab is yours.** A personal table's columns are always yours; an organisation table's need the datatables-management permission the Organisation Admin and Agent Admin roles carry — and ownership either way.

ex-datatables-columns-safely-plan.title: Plan a destructive column change
ex-datatables-columns-safely-plan.task: Plan dropping `opmerking` and retyping `btw_pct` from Text to Number on a table two automations already use — what to check first, which change is more dangerous, what the dialog says, and what happens to the colleague's automation.
criteria: Starts at the "Used by" tab (or the per-column markers) and works out which automation depends on which column before saving anything
Treats both changes as destructive and explains that the retype is the quieter danger: every value is rewritten and anything that does not fit Number is lost
Expects the "This throws away data" dialog, and understands that confirming is required before a drop that an automation depends on is accepted
Says the colleague's automation must be fixed where it lives, and that the colleague is told before the save rather than after
ex-datatables-columns-safely-plan.guidance: Pass an answer that makes "Used by" the first move and treats the dialog as a confirmation rather than a block. Do not pass an answer that only says "take a backup", that assumes the automation repairs itself or is updated automatically, that proposes renaming the column as a safe substitute for dropping it (a rename keeps the key and changes nothing for the automation), or that treats a retype as harmless because no column disappears.

practiceTopic.title: Changing a live table's columns
practiceTopic.summary: How Bee Flow guards a datatable's shape when automations, apps and pages already read it.
facts: The table detail carries the tabs Columns, Rows, Retention, Sharing and Used by; Used by shows a count and lists every automation, app, web page or knowledge base that touches the table, under the headings Where, Does and Last time; Does says "reads", "writes" or "reads and writes".
Removing or retyping a column opens the dialog "This throws away data" with the buttons "Save anyway" and "Keep them"; adding, renaming or reordering a column opens nothing.
A save that drops a column an automation still names is refused until it is confirmed, because the usage index is consulted before the change is carried out.
A concurrent column edit is refused with "Someone else changed these columns while you were editing. Their version is now shown — please make your change again."
Row visibility can be narrowed to "only the person who added it" but never widened back, because that would disclose every existing row retroactively; the answer tells you to make a new table.

Every table already carries id, created_at, updated_at, created_by and org_id and a new column may not take one of those names; the Technical name can never be changed after creation, while a saved column's display name can, because its underlying key stays the same.
A mirrored table's Columns tab says the columns come from the source and cannot be added to, removed, renamed or retyped there; a form's answers columns are the form's questions.

Editing an organisation table's columns needs the datatables-management permission that the Organisation Admin and Agent Admin roles carry; the check is skipped for a personal table, and in both cases you must own the table (its creator, or an organisation administrator of that organisation).

actionChecks.label: Add a column to a table something uses
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Datatables, open a table you own that the "Used by" tab already lists, add a column on the Columns tab and press Save columns.

endpoints.returns: { datatables: [...] } — each row carries id, name, key, scopeKind, ownerUserId, grade and usageCount

criteria.label: A table you own is used by something
criteria.hint: Its Used by tab lists at least one automation, app, web page or knowledge base.
criteria.rule: some row in GET /api/datatables has grade === 'owner' and usageCount > 0
